rv.q: Care at the Young Vic is a profoundly moving, beautifully acted portrait of life, and death, in a nursing home for the elderly.

Zeldin’s latest work means that the London stage now offers the magnificent Linda Bassett, lynchpin of Call the Midwife, as nurse Phyllis Crane, as an unwilling new arrival in a decidedly unglamorous care home.
This recognition of older female actors, not as standalone stars but as a default position for human beings, is another reason to celebrate Zeldin’s work.
It is gruelling, intense and true, with darkly sublime performances from actors playing the residents.
It’s a play that so desperately wants to be moving, but feels calculating, too, in its attempts to stage sadness, that hyper-real style holding us at a distance.

We follow Joan to her final hours as she lies in her room, her body lovingly bathed by Hazel. If I’ve made it all sound dark beyond belief, I’d better stress that at press night there was a good deal of laughter at the rambling conversations, particularly those involving Hayley Carmichael’s sex-obsessed Simone.
This latest work deals with the grand-daddy of these, the very end of life, and it is gruellingly compelling.
The piece is meticulously, unflashily acted by a faultless ensemble, and its situations – minor tragedies, no less shattering for being commonplace – are often heartbreaking.
But Zeldin’s painfully realistic production - offering a panoramic view of the care home - is also, at times, quite dull.
Which is fair enough: it’s a world that little dramatic light gets thrown on – and with the brilliant Bassett as our proxy, it’s a powerfully unsparing guide to the end.
This is an extraordinary piece of theatre.
It is also superbly acted by all concerned.
The huge power is in the simplicity of the way in which it’s expressed in a work that’s as profoundly sobering as it’s strangely uplifting.
Its tender truthfulness makes Care a great play.
Slow, gritty and profoundly moving, it’s also something of a return to form for Zeldin, after his OTT modern twist on the Greek tragedy of Antigone, The Other Place.
Care is a great theatrical achievement just for its attempts to plumb the subconscious of the elderly, rather than treating them merely as objects of sympathy.
Care, on the other hand, while sharing similarities with Here You Go, lasts for an uninterrupted 130 minutes.
Zeldin skilfully avoids sentimentality and even weaves in some lightness, such as the residents’ rambling conversations.
It 's the sort of role which should give every one of us, renewed respect and admiration for the nursing profession and those who commit their lives to it.
Summarised in that way, the play might sound simplistic or even banal; in fact, it is a profound and expert dramatic achievement.

cn.t: Zeldin's unflinching, naturalistic portrait of life in a care home earns widespread acclaim for its humanity and Bassett's powerful performance, though some find its painstaking realism grueling and overly bleak.
